votes.fatal_flaw:
The cheap-right rung is weakened but holds. Three flaws come out of the cheap-right lens.
(1) The 53,686 acres at $1/ac are adversely selected. They are what 18-22 active bidders passed on, including Zanskar, Ormat, Invenergy and usually the nominator itself. Day-after uptake fell from 58% in 2023 to 3.7% in 2025.
(2) ML diffusion is already causing signal collision. 27% of nominated acres were rejected as duplicates (GAO-26-108040), and Zanskar's GeoCore plus the INGENIOUS maps put everyone in the same top decile. Only targets from new labels (the TG archive, released NDOM wells) still clear at the floor.
(3) The neutral-bank model has to leak. Unlike Zanskar, which stays quiet until a PPA, it makes money by showing data rooms to many buyers. Pumpernickel shows the cost: disclosure repriced adjacent land from $2 to $232/ac in about a month, and the discoverer lost it by $1. The 51,200 ac/state cap limits how many whole fairways can be locked before pitching, which bounds the federal book at roughly 0.1-0.5 GW per state (calc from San Emidio's 17,846 ac per 10 MW). That is about 1-3 GW across 6 states, not 10-20 GW.
Separately, the $5/MWh override precedent is a financing royalty (Centaurus paid $75M of preferred equity for it), not a land override. Buyers are long on land: Ormat holds 434k acres and 34 US prospects.
votes.ai_answer_to_flaw:
Lock first, then disclose.
- Use the new-label ML ranking to pick fairways, then lock each whole fairway before any data room opens. Use floor-bid nominations wrapped in decoy nominations (100k ac is about $17k), first-in-time UT/ID state-trust sections, and private fee leases at about $1/ac/yr.
- Run ML defensively as well: score every rival nomination and every leftover parcel, and file only where the new-label model disagrees with the public baseline.
- Sell under NDA to one exclusive buyer per fairway on a Crump-style carry: the developer funds the first $15M plus pays $2.5M cash, with the originator floored at 20%.
- Recycle the cap by assigning working interests while keeping an ORRI. Unitized acreage is excluded from the cap. Whether an ORRI counts toward the cap is unverified.
This rescues the cheap-right rung, because the BLM lease price is fixed once held (no re-appraisal, ministerial transfer). It does not rescue the step-up rung. Value is still realised at a confirmation well plus a PPA (confirmed resource without a PPA is about $0.1M/MW), so the bank must co-carry assets to a confirmation well. That is consistent with the scorer's C4 of 3.

Use AI to move the sale point to where value actually jumps, and to make rights acquisition stealthy:
1. ML ranks prospects. The company carries the top ones to a confirmation well plus an interconnection request and water rights. DOE cost-share (Crump's Phase I got ~80%) and farm-in money pay for the wells.
2. LLM title extraction across courthouse, split-estate and state trust records locks private and state heat rights quietly. Those rights have no 51,200 ac/state federal cap and no public nomination.

This partly rescues the play. It becomes a viable prospect generator carried to confirmation, at roughly $5-20M per confirmation well, not the $17k asset-light bank in the pitch. The pure Black Stone/TPL shape only works at 10+ GW under contract, which needs EGS-grade acreage sold to Fervo-type buyers. No incumbent occupies the neutral role today: Zanskar is an integrated IPP, Ormat and Fervo are owner-operators, Enverus takes no land, and the land-bank LLCs have no data. Unsold leftovers are still unscreened: 26 of 27 unsold Oct 2025 parcels drew no day-after filing, and 53,686 ac remained open at $1/ac.

Wounded, not killed. No buyer pays a big multiple at once for a gradient-hole-confirmed geothermal right. The value jump comes later, at flow test plus PPA plus interconnection, which is 5-8 years out and depends on someone else building. Evidence:
(1) U.S. Geothermal's 2018 sale proxy put about 100 MW of development projects at a ~$10M liquidation value (~$0.1M/MW). Bidder Party G walked away because of those assets, and bankers discounted development projects at 14-16% against 8-10% for operating ones.
(2) Greenfield assets went into Ormat's Terra-Gen (2021) and Enel (2023) deals with no separate price.
(3) The only farm-out template, Crump Geyser, paid the originator just $2.5M in cash over 3 years plus a $15M carry for 50%, and the resource came in marginal (~130C).
(4) The main buyers already make their own land. Ormat holds 434k acres and 34 US prospects; Fervo holds ~596k acres bought at ~$4/ac and has $1.9B of IPO cash. Their exploration teams discount outside data, and well-funded buyers will prefer to buy acreage outright rather than accept overrides.
(5) The $5/MWh 'override precedent' is Centaurus's return on $75M of preferred equity, not a royalty paid for land. The real land-override precedent is ~4% gross on one BLM lease (USG).
(6) Size on hydrothermal alone fails the federal cap. 51,200 ac/state x 6 states is ~307k federal acres. At ~150 ac/MW and under 33% project success, that is roughly 0.5-0.7 GW. Under a $5/MWh override that is ~$20-27M/yr, about $0.3-0.45B at 16x. That is too small, and it arrives a decade out.
(7) Nominations are public and carry no preference right. 27% of nominated acres are duplicates, and land LLCs took ~52% of auction dollars, so the edge leaks.
votes.ai_answer_to_flaw:
The best AI-leveraged answer has four parts:
(a) Don't sell at the gradient-hole stage. Use ML to push the cost of a discovery toward Zanskar's claimed under $15k/MW. Then carry each prospect to a confirmation well using other people's money (DOE cost-share, which reimbursed ~50% at Crump; farm-in carries), so the company sits on the confirmed-resource rung at venture cost.
(b) Add ML over interconnection queues and transmission headroom, and only lock up parcels next to spare capacity. Buyers demonstrably pay for this: Blue Mountain has 51 MW of interconnection on a 20 MW plant, and Terra-Gen came with a 300-400 MW line. That turns 'confirmed, no PPA' (~$0.1M/MW) into 'confirmed plus interconnection', the rung R10 says buyers pay for.
(c) Get around the cap and the copying by making state first-file and private/split-estate leases the core of the book. Private and subleased land is 18% of Ormat's acreage, has no per-state cap and is not publicly nominated. BLM noncompetitive filing at $1/ac stays a sideline.
(d) Make size come from EGS-grade acreage. Fervo-type density is ~15 ac/MW, so ~300k+ acres could underlie 10-20 GW. That is the ~$5-10B royalty-book case at FNV/RGLD-like 16-22x, helped by the 2025 law making geothermal income MLP-qualifying.
Verdict: this rescues size on plausibility, as standing rules allow. It does NOT rescue 'big multiple at once'. Cash comes from carries and overrides on assets other companies build, not from day-one sales, so the business looks like Black Stone (development agreements with minimum commitments), not like a flipper. A pure flipper caps out near EMX's ~$444M.

The step-up rung is the weak point. The size rung is not. Five problems with the step-up:

(1) No buyer has ever paid a multiple for unproven private or Texas EGS land. Every disclosed comp is western BLM hot-play land ($344-410/ac max bids in 2025; $232/ac step-out after Zanskar's PR) or a built, contracted plant (Ormat paid $4.3-5.6M/MW). B02 finds "no public, arm's-length market for proven-but-unbuilt geothermal resources."

(2) The headline step-up mis-uses Fervo's ~$12.9k/acre mark. That is the IPO valuation divided by acreage, so it is a mark on a developer with 658 MW of PPAs, not a land price. Fervo's 424B4 says buyers pay for screening quality and transmission access: rivals "paid hundreds of dollars per acre ... for positions that failed to meet our development standards." It names only federal land and does not mention Texas or Oklahoma.

(3) EGS's selling point is that it can be sited almost anywhere, and that erodes land scarcity in exactly the places this play targets. Texas gross EGS potential is 14,578 GW (Aljubran & Horne). The scarce 0.27% of US land where 4 km or less is optimal is "mostly in the West", not in TX or OK. In the NREL 2050 state build table, Texas gets only 3.1 GW, against CA 27.9 and LA 10.5.

(4) Revealed preference: Sage, the Texas-native champion, took its next commercial EGS plant to Ormat's Blue Mountain in Nevada (Sep 2026), and Meta's two 150 MW geothermal deals are with Sage and XGS (New Mexico). Fervo (596k acres, ~256k of them idle) and Ormat (434k acres) screen and lease for themselves. Raser held 250k+ acres and its equity was wiped out: a land bank with no buyer goes to zero.

(5) Timing: EGS builds take 5-10 years, so a $5/MWh override pays cash in the 2030s.

On size, $1B+ is plausible but not immediate. 2-3 GW under override at about $39M/yr per GW, valued at 10-30x (Viper 9.5x to TPL 31.8x EV/EBITDA), gives about $1-3B. $5-10B needs 10-20 GW, which is more than the whole NREL Texas allocation.

The play fails the "big multiple paid at once" test. No arm's-length sale of a confirmed-but-unbuilt geothermal resource has ever been priced. In its 2017 review, USG's board valued about 100 MW of development projects at "about $10M liquidation value" (about $0.1M/MW), and bidder Party G walked away because of those assets. Ormat took greenfields such as Coyote Canyon (Terra-Gen 2021) and two Enel sites (2023) inside larger deals and priced them at zero. A buyer only pays real money at the PPA or operating stage, at $4.3-5.6M/MW.

The 2-5% royalty in the plan also collides with the existing royalty stack. The landowner already takes 2-5% of gross (stepping 3 to 4 to 5% at Neal Hot Springs). BLM takes 1.75% and then 3.5%. Ormat's blended royalty burden is only about 4.5% of electricity revenue. An extra 2-5% override on top would push the total to 6-13%, so the realistic override is about 1-2% or $1-5/MWh. Using 7,884 MWh per MW-yr (90% capacity factor), 2% of $100/MWh is about $16k/MW-yr (my arithmetic). That is worth about $0.17M/MW at an 8% discount rate over 25 years, or about $0.1M/MW once you allow for the 5-8 years before the plant runs.

Size (my arithmetic): a $1B royalty book needs about $60-100M/yr of royalty at a 10-16x multiple. At a 2% override that means about 4-6 GW operating under it. At $5/MWh it still means about 2-2.5 GW. Fee land is only 18-27% of developer acreage. Ormat and Fervo already sign private leases with their own landmen, and Fervo built its land position at about $4/acre. The whole existing US geothermal royalty pool is about $45M/yr. Raser held 250k+ acres and its equity went to zero in 2011.

The multiple on cost is huge (about $5/acre in against roughly $0.1M/MW of value), but the cash is small and arrives late. As written, this is a hydrothermal ranch bank that sells royalties. It looks like a prospect generator, which caps out in the hundreds of millions (EMX was about $444M), not a $1B+ company.
